Slck PSUs 
*362. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR : W ill the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government propose to take the sick PSUs out of the 
purview of Board for Industrial and Financial Reconstruction (BIFR) to 
facilitate easy liquidation and faster rehabilitation; 
(b) whether there are plans to scrap the BIFR under the proposed 
Company Law Amendment; 
(c) whether Government have recently issued directives to sick PSUs to 
clear outstanding dues of the employees within 45 days; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) A Statement is placed on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
It is proposed to repeal the Sick Industrial Companies (Special 
Provisions) Act (SICA) and wind up the Board of Industrial and Financial 
Reconstruction (BIFR). An alternative mechanism for liquidation and 
rehabilitation of sick companies has been provided in the Companies Act 
through the Companies (Second Amendment) Act, 2002, which will also 
provide for establishing the National Company Law Tribunal. Under the 
amended Act, an Government company is exempt from the mandatory 
provision for making reference to the Tribunal, other than, with the prior 
approval of the Central or the State Government, as the case may be. 
Administrative Ministries of sick PSUs having outstanding statutory dues 
have been advised to clear them within 45 days, out of their own resources. 
Other loss making and sick PSUs which have outstanding dues, but may not 
have the resources have been advised to expedite clearance of dues by 
disposal of surplus/non-performing a ssets. For enterprises that neither have 
the capacity to clear the dues out of their internal resources nor have 
disposable surplus assets, the Ministries have been advised to frame revival/ 
closure plans.

agreement among the Government of Orissa, Government  of Chhattisgarh

Closing of Central Water Commission 
†*371. SHRI BASHISTHA NARAIN SI NGH: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) the main tasks of the Central Water Commission; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the ta sk for development of water resources

to water resources is executed by the State; and

THE MINISTER OF WATER R ESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) Central Water Commission is an apex technical organization in 
the field of water resources development  in the country and is the main 
technical arm of the Ministry of Wate r Resources. Central Water Commission 
(CWC) is involved with following tasks: 
Resource assessment; macro level planning; project planning including 
hydrological studies, designs, environmental and rehabilitation & resettlement 
issues; project evaluation; extending

advice on planning and design problems, execution of water resources 
development projects and project monitoring; operational flood forecasting & 
dam safety aspects in operation of water resources projects; research and 
development; standardization and documentation; guidance/advisory role in 
report of committees, boards etc. and technical support to different Ministries. 
(b) (i) As per the Seventh Schedule of the Constitution, Entry 
17 of List-ll (State List), "Water that is to say, water supplies, 
irrigation and canals, drainage a nd embankments, water storage and 
water power subject to the provisions of Entry 56 of List I" is with 
the State Governments. 
However, as per Entry 56 of Li st-I (Union List) "Regulation and 
development of inter-state rivers and river valleys to the extent to which such 
regulation and development under the co ntrol of the Union is declared by 
Parliament by law to be expedient in the public interest" is with the Union 
Government. 
From the above it is clear that t he regulation and development of inter-
state rivers is the primary responsibi lity of the Union Government for which 
Central Water Commission extends nece ssary technical support to the 
Government. 
Central Water Commission works on specialized areas of macro level 
planning in water resources development sector which comes under Entry 20 
of List-Ill (Concurrent List) on "Economic and social planning". It performs 
technical tasks with respect to respon sibility of the Central Government on 
Inter-State Boards and Inter-State Water Disputes. 
(c) In view of the present func tions of CWC and constitutional 
provisions as enumerated at (a) and (b) above, it is necessary to 
continue the CWC to discharge sove reign functions of the Union. 
In fact, it will be required to play a more important & pro-active 
role in view of incr easing Inter-State i ssues in river basin 
management, and development needs in water sector of the country 
as well las increasing international emphasis on water related 
issues.

*377. SHRI JIBON ROY: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND COMPANY 
AFFAIRS be pleased to state:

forego Rs. 1400 crores as a result of bailout package to three steel companies 
namely, Essar Steel, Ispat Industries and Jindal Vijaynagar Steel; and

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) and (b) No, Sir. Under the aegis of the Corporate Debt 
Restructuring (CDR) mechanism instituted by the Reserve Bank of India, the 
CDR Empowered Group has worked out a package for the Steel Industry. 
Essar Steel Limited, Ispat Industries Limited and Jindal Vijayanagar Steel 
Limited have availed of this package. The terms and conditions of the 
package include writing down of equity by the borrowers and furnishing of 
personal guarantees. The salient features  of the restructuring by lenders are 
as follows: 
(i) The new rupee loan would carry interest rate of 14% p.a. as 
against the higher document rate. 
39 

RAJYA  SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
(ii) Foreign Currency (FC) Loans: The FC loans sanctioned 
originally to these companies continue to earn the interest rates 
as stipulated in the agreements and there is no sacrifice on 
these loans. 
(iii) As per the restructuring pa ckage, 40% of the rupee loans are 
converted into foreign currency loans carrying a fixed interest 
rate of 8% p.a. 
(iv) The compound interest overdues are to be converted into zero 
coupon debentures. 
(v) The charges by way of liquidated damages and penal interest 
over and above the compound interest are to be waived. 
(vi) Part of the loans are being converted into equity capital of the 
companies. This conversion would take place after the existing 
equity capital of the companies is written down by 40%.

Impact of economic recession on industrial sector 
2658. SHRI CO. POULOSE: Will the Minister of FINANCE AND 
COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the possibilities of industrial recovery are taking a beating 
with global economic recession continuing unabated; 
(b) whether it is a fact that the grow th of services sector has also been 
adversely effected by the global economic recession; 
(c) whether Government are aware t hat the growth of the services 
sector is contingent upon healthy agricul tural and industrial sectors and with 
the declaration or stagnancy of these sectors the growth of the services 
sector is going to be seriously affected; and 
(d) if so, the steps Government have taken in this regard? 
75 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (d) No, Sir. There is no evidence of any adverse 
impact of global recession on the performa nce of industrial sector as well as 
services sector, rather industry has stimulated overall growth, despite a 
decline in agriculture. As per the latest data on Index of Industrial Production 
(IIP) released by Central Statistical Or ganisation (CSO) industrial production 
registered a growth of 5.5% during Ap ril-January 2002-03 as compared to 
2.6% in the same period last year. Se rvices sector is also growing at a 
reasonably good pace. Exports are also growing at a rate faster than that 
targeted. The latest figures on expor ts for April-February 2002-03 show an 
impressive increase of 16.7% and the manufactured exports constitute around 
80% of total exports from India. Other  indicators of industrial performance 
namely, growth in six infrastructure industries, capital goods, foreign 
exchange reserves and non-food credit  continue to register good growth 
rates. The Government of India has  taken a number of steps including 
enhancement of allocations towards some of the major schemes, which will 
boost demand, especially in construction, housing, steel and cement sectors. 
To improve operating enviroment of the industry and to boost its 
competitiveness, the Government has enacted several laws.

Tighter accountability norms for banks 
2690. SHRI RAMA MUNI REDDY SIR IGIREDDY: Will the Minister of 
FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that the RB I is seriously thinking of bringing 
tighter accountability norms for banks; 
(b) if so, what is the main idea behind bringing tighter accountability 
norms for all banks in the country; and 
(c) whether Government propose to bring an amendment to the 
existing laws in this regard? 
THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) to (c) The Reserve Bank of India (RBI) had 
constituted an Expert Committee on Lega l Aspects of Bank Frauds under the 
Chairmanship of Dr. N.L. Mitra, Vice Chancellor, National Law University, 
Jodhpur. The Committee submitted its report  to the RBI in two parts. Part I 
dealing with in-house preventive measures and part II dealing with prohibitive 
aspects requiring legislative changes for its implementation. The 
recommendations of the Committee cont ained in part I are Development of 
Best Practice Code (BPC), system of internalisation of BPC, internal check 
and internal control, legal complianc e certification in all transactions 
exceeding a value limit, legal compliance audit, data building on the exercise 
of discretionary power and monitoring th ereof, liability of the accounting and 
auditing profession etc. These recomme ndations were accepted by RBI. All 
Scheduled Commercial Banks were advised to implement them. In part II of 
its report, the Mitra Committee had sugge sted for a separate statute styled 
"Financial Fraud Investigation, Prosecut ion, Recovery and Restoration of 
Property Act, 2001". The Committee has also suggested certain amendments 
to the Indian Penal Code, Criminal Procedure Code and Indian Evidence Act. 
The RBI has accepted the above recommendations and have referred the

THE MINISTER OF FINANCE AND COMPANY AFFAIRS (SHRI 
JASWANT SINGH): (a) The National Securities Depository Limited (NSDL) 
follows a two-tier fee structure i.e. NSDL levies fees on its Depository 
Participants (DPs), while DPs charge their clients. NSDL's charges are 
uniform across all DPs. The DPs are free to levy their own tariff structure 
based on the services provided by them . The major fee that is charged by

Charges, which ranges anywhere from Rs. 200/- to Rs. 600/- per annum.

DPs are free to levy their own tariff structure or effect changes in the tariff 
structure with a 30 days notice period to  their clients. The Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (SEBI) and the NS DL do not keep the data of tariff 
charged by the DPs as they are not required to report to them. 
(c) The fee structure of DPs is a commercial issue between them and 
their clients. However, as per the agreement signed with their clients, a 
minimum of 30 days' notice is required to  be given by. the DPs to their clients 
whenever the fee structure is revised. At any point of time, an investor can 
shift from one DP to another, in case the investor so desires.

Water shortage in developing countries 
2771. SHRIMATI BIMBA RAIKAR: Will the Minister of WATER 
RESOURCES be pleased to state: 
(a) whether a recent study by FA O(UN) has predicted severe water 
shortage in developing countries; 
(b) whether according to the report the water problem will aggravate to 
the extent that every one country am ong the five developing countries will 
face acute water scarcity; 
(c) whether India participated in the World Water Forum conclave held 
in Kyoto during March 2003; and 
(d) if so, a summary of the deliberations held at the conclave? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) As per a new study by FAO (UN) titled 'Unlocking the water 
potential of agriculture, published on the eve of the Third World Water Forum 
in Kyoto, it is stated inter-alia that farmers in developing countries will face 
increasing competition for scarce freshwater resources from industry and 
domestic users. It further states that whil e there is no global water crises, the 
serious water and food security problems in some developing countries and 
regions need to be urgently addressed. 
(b) Yes, Madam. 
(c) Yes, Madam. An Indian delegation led by Shri Arjun Charan Sethi, 
Minister of Water Resources participated in the Third World Water Forum held 
in Osaka, Shiga and Kyoto, Japan during March, 2003. 
(d) The 3rd World Water Forum met from 16-23rd March, 2003 in 
Kyoto, Osaka and Shiga, Japan. On this  occasion, two Ministerial meetings, 
namely Irrigation Ministers' meet on "W ater Food and Agriculture" and main 
Ministerial Conference were organized on 21st March and 22-23 March 
respectively. 
During the ministerial meeting on "Water, Food and Agriculture", a 
presentation was made by Secretary (WR) highlighting its achievements in the 
field of agriculture, water resources development 
185 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
and management alongwith action which needs to be taken to solve 
agriculture water issues in our country. In this regard, need for building dams 
to augment water supplies for food security and poverty alleviation as well as 
imperative need for transfer of water from surplus areas to deficit areas was 
expressed. A Ministerial declarati on, which was earlier negotiated after 
prolonged discussions by senior officers, was adopted on 21st March, 2003. It 
outlines a plan for action to modernize and improve agriculture use, increase 
water prodcutivity, promote better governance, consider environmental 
aspects, undertake research and deve lopment and foster international 
cooperation. 
In the main ministerial declaration adopted in the final plenary session 
on 23rd March, statement was made on  General Policy, Water Resources 
Management and Benefit Sharing, Safe Drinking Water and Sanitation, Water 
for Food and Rural Development, Water Pollution Prevention and Ecosystem 
Conservation and Disaster Mitigation and Risk Management. 
Minister (WR) chaired one of t he five sub-groups session of the 
ministerial conference where issue of  "Water Resources Management and 
Benefit Sharing* was discussed. This session was attended by 
Ministers/representatives of  62 countries, one region and eight International 
Organizations. 
In this sub-group meeting, the nee d to develop dams for irrigation, 
storages, flood control and hydro-electric  energy with due consideration to 
environmental and social impact as well as sound resettlement plans was 
brought out. It also underscored the need for international financial assistance 
for capacity building & technology transfer. It also urged the need for good 
governance and confidence-building measures and emphasized the 
requirement to increase the use of innovative and appropriate technologies 
such as desalination and re-use of treated water. 
Apart from the Senior Officials' Me etings for finalization of Draft 
Declaration and the Ministerial Conferen ce in which the Declarations were 
adopted, there were many Sessions, some of them running parallel, organized 
at Kyoto, Shiga and Osaka.

187

commitment of improving its quality,  as revealed in the World Water 
Development Report; 
(b) if so, the details in this regard; and 
(c) if so, what long-term steps Gove rnment propose to adopt regarding 
adequacy of water supply in the country and improving its quality? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER RESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. As per  the 'United Nations World Water 
Development Report-Water for people, Water for Life', India has been ranked 
120th among 122 selected nations in the world in terms of quality of water. 
Belgium is at 122th rank. The report states that the indicators like the 
widespread occurance of poor water quality, the diversion of water from 
natural aquatic ecosystems and the emerging problems with ground water 
recharge were noted for indications of relative water quality. 
(c) Water being a State subject, water resources schemes including the 
schemes to overcome the shortage of water resources are formulated, 
planned, executed and funded by the c oncerned State Governments. To help 
the State Governments in their effort s to harness the water from natural 
resources and accelerate creation of irrigation potential by early completion of 
ongoing schemes, Government of India has launched Accelerated Irrigation 
Benefits Programme (AIBP) since 1996-97 to provide central loan assistance. 
Government of India is promoting rainwater harvesting through 
Watershed Mangement Programme, artificial recharge of ground water rooftop 
rainwater harvesting under the sector reform project of Accelerated Rural 
Water Supply Programme under the Ministry of Rural Development, for which 
technical and financial assistance is provided to the State Governments and 
other implementing agencies. The Governm ent of India also assists the State 
Governments by providing financial assistance under Accelerated Rural Water 
Supply Programme (ARWSP) for rural drinking water and under Command 
Area Development Programme to increase efficiency in utilisation of irrigation 
water. Central Ground Water Board has also taken up a 
188 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA   SABHA 
Central Sector Scheme on "Studies of Recharge to Ground Water" on pilot 
basis. 
For meeting future requirements of water, as a long term measure, 
National Water Development Agency have formulated National Perspective 
Plan for water resources development which envisages interlinking between 
various Peninsular rivers and Himalayan rivers for transfer of water from 
surplus basins to water deficit basins which will accrue benefits of drinking 
water supply, irrigation, hydro-power, flood control, navigation, fisheries, 
salinity and pollution control etc. 
Several steps have been taken for improvement/restoration of quality of 
water bodies in the country and some of them are : 
(i) Ensuring industries, located on the banks of rivers and lakes, set 
up the requisite pollution control facilities. 
(ii) Issuance of Directives to the defaulting industries for preventing 
discharge to untreated waste water into water bodies. 
(iii) Formulation and implementation of National River and Lake 
Conservation Plan for restoration of water quality of the rivers 
and lakes.

Rehabilitation package for Sardar Sarovar Dam Oustees 
2777. DR. AKHILESH DAS: Will th e Minister of WATER RESOURCES 
be pleased to state: 
(a) the progress made so far in the cosntruction of the Sardar Sarovar 
Project, the expenditure so far incurred and the share of co st contributed by 
each participating State; 
(b) whether Gujarat had agreed to a revised rehabilitation package of 
Rs. 239 crores for the dam oustees of Madhya Pradesh and to provide free 
electricity to Madhya Pradesh in lieu of the power loss likely to arise as a 
result of the Irrigation By-Pass Tunnel (IBPT) constructed without 
concurrence of the participating States; and 
(c) if so, how far Gujarat has carried out and financed the 
rehabilitation package, as per agreement? 
THE MINISTER OF WATER R ESOURCES (SHRI ARJUN CHARAN 
SETHI): (a) The progress made so far in the construction of the Sardar 
Sarovar Project as below : 
Dam: The spillway blocks of the Sard ar Sarovar dam (block No. 30 to 
46) have been raised up to Elevation 95 metre. 3 metre high humps have also 
been constructed over block Nos. 31 to  45 of this truncated portion of the 
spillway keeping in view the safety of  the dam. Other blo cks are at various 
higher levels. 
Power House : The canal Head Power House of the project is 
completed in all respects and test run for some units has also been done. The 
works of River Bed Power House are in progress. 
Canals : The canal lining works in the reach 0 to 263 Km of Narmada 
Main Canal are almost complete and the remaining reach upto Rajasthan 
border is under various stages of construction. 
Expenditure: An amount of rs. 14, 056.46 crore has been spent on the 
construction of the Sardar Sarovar Project upto 31st January, 2003. The 
share of cost received from the Governemnts of Madhya Pradesh, 
Maharashtra and Rajasthan is Rs. 78 1.53 crore, Rs. 478.44 crore and Rs. 
125.95 crore respectively. 
(b) As per the information received from the Sardar Sarovar Narmada 
Nigam Limited, the Government of Gujarat had agreed to an additional 
liberalized rehabilitation package and financial assitance of Rs. 201 crore for 
the displaced families of the project in Madhya 
193 

RAJYA SABHA [8 April, 2003] 
Pradesh Pradesh. The issue of construction of irrigation Bye-Pass Tunnel 
(IBPT) at Sardar Sarovar Project had been discussed among the Chief 
Ministers of Gujarat and Madhya Pr adesh and Ministers of Rajasthan and 
Maharashtra Accordingly the Chief Minister of Madhya Pradesh is 
compensated at free of cost for the loss of hydro power for all the water 
passing through IBPT and this loss should be converted into the million units 
of energy lost. Based on these discussions, the Review Committee of 
Narmada Control Authority in its 9th meeting held on 18-08-2001 decided that; 
1. The Narmada Control Authority (NCA) decision on IBPT is endorsed 
and the construction of IBPT should be completed. 
2. Government of Gujarat shall co mpensate Government of Madhya 
Pradesh, free of cost, for the loss of power due to running of IBPT, 
which will be calculated in million units. 
3. The reservoir water level shall not be depleted below the Minimum 
Draw Down Level (MDDL) of elevation 110.64 metre. 
4. The NCA shall evolve a mechanism to control and ensure that the 
reservoir water is not drawn through the IBPT below the MDDL. 
(c) As per the request of the Gove rnment of Madhya Pradesh, the 
Government of Gujarat has provided Rs. 165 crore to the government of 
Madhya Pradesh as rehabilitation package to expedite the Ressettlement & 
Rehabilitation works in Madhya Pradesh as per the information provided by 
the Sardar Sarovar Narmada Nigam Limited.

SPECIAL MENTIONS 
NEED FOR CLEARANCE OF PENDING IRRIGATION PROJECTS 
OF ANDHRA PRADESH WITH THE CENTRAL GOVERNMENT 
DR. T. SUBBARAMI REDDY (Andhra Pradesh): Three proposals (1) 
Janjhvati; (2) Velingonda and (3) Hyderabad Water Supply Scheme are 
pending with the Central Government for approval since 1992,  1997 and 
1998. 
210 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
1. Janjhvati Project: 
This project envisages to utilize 4 TMC of water of river Janjhvati to 
provide irrigation in 24,636 acres of land in vlzianagaram district. The project 
was formulated on the basis of an inter-State agreement signed between the 
States of Orissa and Andhra Pradesh in  1976 to utilize waters of Janjhvati 
river. 
2. Velingonda Project: 
Velingonda project envisages to draw 40 TMC of flood water of the 
river Krishna from Srisailam reservoir through the Naliamala hills to provide 
irrigation in 4.38 lakh acres of land in  the drought prone area of Prakasam 
district.  The Ministry of Environment and Forests has given its clearance. 
3. Hyderabad Water supply and sanitation project: 
To provide adequate drinking water to a population of 50 lakhs in 
Hyderabad, the State Government formulated a scheme of lifting 16.5 TMC of 
water from the foreshore of Nagarjunasagar reservoir on the inter-State river 
Krishna. This scheme will be funded by the World Bank and requires a 
clearance from CWC. The water for this scheme is proposed by AP for 
utilization from out of its allocation under KWDT award. 
As all these projects are impor tant and are pending with the 
Government of India for long, hence requ ire early clearance, so that these 
projects are implemented for the benefit of people of Andhra Pradesh. Thank 
you. 
DEMAND FOR WITHDRAWAL OF TEN PER CENT EXCISE DUTY 
ON POWERLOOM FABRICS 
SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Nadu): The powerloom industry in 
Tamil Nadu is in a very bad state of affairs. The latest blow has come due to 
the imposition of 10 per cent excise  duty on powerloom fabric which was 
recently announced in the current Budget. 
The powerloom owners in the State were already undergoing an 
ordeal, in view of the recessionary trend and a sluggish demand for their 
products. In the present trend to boost the powerloom sector industries and to 
improve the means of livelihood of mil lions of people, the Centre should 
seriously consider the withdrawal of new excise levy. The powerloom 
industries should be permitted to adopt the optional excise duty which is in 
vogue now.   If it is not possible due to the prevailing economic 
211 

RAJYA SABHA        [8 April, 2003] 
scenario, at least, those whose turnover is less than Rs.1 crore should be 
exempted from the new levy. 
In view of the prevailing circumst ances and the difficulties faced by 
the powerloom sector, the Chief Minister of Tamil Nadu has written a letter to 
the hon. Prime Minister to reconsider the new excise levy at the earliest. 
I, therefore, strongly urge upon t he Government to withdraw the 
excise duty of 10 per cent on powerloom fabrics, at the earliest, so as to revive 
the powerloom sector and render justice.   Thank you.

NEED FOR CHANGING NORMS FOR CENTRALLY-SPONSORED 
ACCELERATED URBAN WATER SUPPLY PROGRAMME 
SHRIMATI SHABANA AZMI (Nominated): Sir, it is a matter of great 
shame that five decades after independence we still have not been able to 
give drinking water to all our people. My Special Mention is about the 
Centrally-Sponsored Accelerated Water Supply Programme in Maharashtra 
This scheme is a Centrally-s ponsored programme. As per 1991 
Census, there were 79 towns having less than 20,000 population in 
Maharashtra. Thirty-six proposals were sent to the Union Government. The 
Union Government approved 20 proposals. Out of that, water supply has 
started under 13 schemes and the work on the remaining 7 is in progress. 
The Government of India has not approved the remaining 16 
schemes, although the State Government  has already started the work on 
these schemes. Now, these schemes have been omitted from the AUWSP.

changes:-

water supply limit from 70 litres to 100 litres per day per person. 
The above changes were discussed at the meeting held on 4 th and 
5th July, 1996 and all the Chief Mini sters of States had recommended the 
changes. 
The Maharashtra Chief Minister has been writing letters to the Prime 
Minister of India on the subject. The Working Group constituted by the 
Government of India in August, 1996 had also recommended changes in the 
norms.    The proposals were discussed at a meeting held under the

of India, on 8 th June, 2001. The Government of India has not yet given

norms suggested by Maharashtra Government, which had been supported by 
all the Chief Ministers, so that t he schemes can be implemented by the 
Government of Maharashtra.  Thank you.

ACUTE RESPIRATORY SYNDROME (SARS) 
SHRIMATI N.P.DURGA (Andhra Prades h) : Sir, my special mention 
is about panic over spread of myster y disease, SARS. A new disease known 
as Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome and closely resembles influenza is 
suspected to be a mutant. It starts with high fever, sore throat and cough, but 
has been found to turn fatal when it develops into full-fledged pneumonia. The 
city of Hong Kong has been hit with SARS claiming maximum number of lives 
there and in China also. This disease has spread to South-East Asian 
countries creating a panic like situat ion. It has spread to Canada, Brazil and 
other countries also. So far. this virus has infected 2,300 people in 14 
countries. About 80 people have died. Since China is our neighbouring 
country, we have to be on our guard. Up till now, doctors and WHO could not 
find a diagnose to this disease. 
This has affected business and there is a slump in tourist arrivals. 
This is having a negative im pact on the business. It is sad to learn that WHO 
had little information on what causes SAR S. I think the Government of India 
have taken some measures to alert our airports to check the suspected 
passengers coming from South-East Asian countries and alerted hospitals and 
immunology institutions for treating patients. We have to educate the people of 
India that the disease will not spread if we maintain good hygiene and make 
everyone aware of it through good health education through electronic and 
print media. God forbid, if such a dis ease strikes our country, the Government 
of India should be prepared to tackle it on a war footing.

Boudh. Similarly, the number of tigers of  rare species is coming down year by 
year. Poachers use poison and guns to ki ll' these protected animals for tiger 
skins. In the Similipal Tiger Sanctuary only 99 tigers are seen at present.   The 
total number of tigers in

SHRI PRASANTA CHATTERJEE : Madam, Deputy Chairman, this is 
an important Bill. It has been stated in the Statement of Objects and Reasons 
of the Bill, "In order to safeguard t he interests of the sugarcane growers, 
producers of sugar and the general public , to restabilise the market price of 
sugar and to overcome the difficulties ar ising from the said  challenge.-..this 
amendment Bill is necessary."   It has also been said that the

At the very outset, I would like to emphasize here that we, in the Left, 
have always advocated and taken a stand so that not only sugar but also all 
the essential commodities, including some essential medicines, can be made 
available to the common people at a reas onable control price through the Fair 
Price Shops. Everybody knows that we  have drawn the attention of the 
Government and the people to various  acts and methods. And, the main

been weakened. For whose interest? It has been the practice of the. 
Government to say, "Go to the open ma rket, and face the competition there." 
On the other hand, the grow ers, the actual growers, have not received a fair 
price, and the common consumers have  not received the commodity at a 
reasonable price. Here lies the danger. Even in the case of sugar, at one point 
of time, 60 per cent was levy sugar an d 40 per cent was free sugar. Then, it

sugar at reasonable prices. But our intention is that, as has been written in the 
aims and objects, the public distribution  system should be strengthened. It 
should be ensured that sugar is availa ble at a reasonable price through fair 
price shops. .So, our observation is that the Government orders and the 
directions in this regard should ensu re that the sugarcane growers get a 
reasonable price and the common people also get sugar at a reasonable price 
through fair price shops. These are our observations and demands. With these 
few words, I support this Bill.

SHRIMATI N.P. DURGA (Andhr a Pradesh): Madam Deputy 
Chairperson, it gives me great pleasure to speak on this small piece of 
legislation, moved by the hon. Mini ster for Consumer Affairs, Food and 
Public distribution. The Bill is brou ght before us to amend the Essential 
Commodities Act to plug the loopholes with the help of which some of the 
sugar mills are indulging in malpractices and are selling more sugar in the 
open market than prescribed by the Government, resulting in decline in the 
payment of price to sugarcane growers. The problem arose because the sugar 
release mechanism is governed not directly by the Essential Commodities Act, 
but by the Sugar (Control) Order, 1966.  Taking advantage 
228 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
of this, some of the mills went to c ourt and got decree in their favour under 
article 19 and 14 of the Constitution because clauses 4 and 5 of the Sugar 
(Control) Order are not in conformity with articles 14 and 19 (1) (9) of the 
Constitution. I welcome the inclusion of new clauses, 3(d) and 3(e), in the Act, 
which plugs this loophole and helps the producers of sugarcane to get the 
minimum support price decided by the Government. This is the simple 
amendment that the Government has brought before the House for its 
approval.   It is a good decision. 
But, at the same time, the sugar mills are also facing a tot of 
problems. We all know that sugar i ndustry is the second-largest agro-based 
industry in the country, and the largest industry located in rural areas. We 
have more than half a thousand sugar factories in the country, and the annual 
production is around 190 lakh tonnes. As  of today, the sugar mills are facing 
compound losses to the tune of Rs. 5,500 crores. This industry is facing losses 
for the last three years because of exce ssive production. One of the problems 
that this industry is facing is with regard to the minimum support price of 
sugarcane, which is going up year after year. Tax, power and water charges, 
transportation charges are all going up and the result is that  the production 
cost of sugar is also going up. The other problem is the technology that we are 
using is obsolete. For this, we have to find out some innovative techniques so 
as to reduce the cost of production. If yo u look at other countries, the cost of 
production of one tonne sugar comes to Rs. 9,975/-. whereas in India it is Rs. 
13,700/-! So, there is. nearly, a differ ence of Rs. 4,oooA per tonne in the 
production cost alone. I agree that the countries such as Brazil, USA, Japan, 
and some European countries are giving subsidy. But, the technology that has 
been adopted there is far more advanc ed than the technology that we are 
using here. So. I would like to know from the hon. Minister what his Ministry is 
doing to reduce the cost of production of sugar. 
The other worrying issue is that the exports are also coming down. I 
will just give one example. Last year, we had exported about 11.5 million 
tonnes of sugar, whereas this year, the exports slumped to 10 million tonnes. 
So, I would like to know from the hon. Minister how is he going to export more 
sugar to other countries and deal with the exorbitant import duties imposed by 
some of the developed countries? I would also like to know from the hon. 
Minister the impact of Iraq War on our ex port of sugar. I suggest that when 
other countries are imposing more and more import duty, why can't India do 
the same and save our sugar mills, which are on 
229 

RAJYA SABHA              [8 April, 2003] 
the verge of collapse. By imposing a heavy import duty on sugar, we can 
reduce sugar imports and, thereby, redu ce piling up of sugar stocks in the 
country. 
The next point is this. Is it true that  the Indian Sugar Mills Association 
is demanding for retaining tax on sugar, excise duty, central cess on sugar and 
excise duty on molasses for a short period of one year, in the light of the 
pathetic condition in which the sugar indus try is passing through? If yes; what 
is the Government doing In this regard? 
Finally, I wish to bring to the notice of the hon. Minister that Brazil and 
other developed countries are allowing about 10-15 per cent ethanol to be 
mixed with petrol, whereas we are allowing only 5 per cent of ethanol to be 
mixed with petrol. Hence, I request the hon. Minister to increase this to, at 
least, 15 per cent. This will not only result in savings in our oil import bill, but 
also add to the commercial viability of our sugar mills. Above all, the sugarcane 
farmer will get a higher price for his produce and, at the same time, the losses 
that are being suffered by sugar mills in the country could be minimised. 
I would also like to know what the Ministry is doing with regard to 
producing electricity with the waste that comes out of sugar mills. 
I want the hon. Minister to respond to the queries raised by me. 
Thank you.

SHRI P.G. NARAYANAN (Tamil Na du): Madam Deput y Chairman, 
the Essential Commodities Act, 1955 provides for maintaining or increasing 
supplies of essential commodities or for securing their equitable distribution 
and availability at fair prices. The Central Government may issue orders 
regulating or prohibiting the producti on, supply and distribution of such 
essential commodities in trade and commerce. The present Bill aims to 
amend Section 3 of the Act. The new Sections 3(d) and 3(e) have been 
introduced. This amendment has to be  read with Sugar Control Order, 1966. 
This amendment has been brought forth keeping in mind the policy of partial 
control of sugar since 1966 and allocating a portion of sugar as levy sugar for 
the Public Distribution System. We ar e very well aware that the Central 
Government has adopted a regulated release mechanism for release of levy 
free sugar, that is. free sale sugar by issuing orders under the Sugar Control 
Order, 1966. As per new amendments, a ccording to the directions of the 
Central Government, a producer can import, export, dispose of, deliver or 
remove any kind of sugar from the bounded godowns of the factory. While 
implementing this Section, we should see to it that it does not affect the 
pledging of such sugar by the producer in favour of any scheduled bank. 
Madam, the Sugar Control Order was la st amended in June 1999. Clause 4 
and clause 5 of the said Order empowered the Government to give direction 
to the producer, on lines similar to the new amendment, that is, Sections 3(d) 
and 3(e) of the Essential Commodities B ill. I very well understood the recent 
challenge the Government is facing to the regulated release mechanism in the 
courts, which has led to the difficulties in its operation. Due to the difficulties in 
operating there, there is a sharp decline in the sugar prices also, which in turn, 
affects the capacity of t he producer to pay cane prices to the sugarcane 
growers. Please, ensure that these pr ovisions will definitely safeguard the 
interests of the sugarcane growers,  producers and general public. The 
present amendments are aimed at re-sta bilising the market prices of sugar 
and to overcome the difficulties

THE REPRESENTATION OF THE PEOPLE (AMENDMENT) BILL. 2001 
THE MINISTER OF LAW AND JU STICE (SHRI ARUN JAlTLEY): 
Madam, I move: 
That the BilI further to amend the Representation of the People Act, 
1951, be taken into consideration." 
Madam, the thrust of this Bill relates to two special aspects with 
regard to the procedure for elections to the Members of the Council of States 
i.e. the Rajya Sabha. We have since 1951 had a firm system where to be 
eligible under section 3 of the Represent ation of the People Act, to contest for 
the election for the Rajya Sabha, one has to be an elector of that State; and 
under section 19 of the Act, in order to be an elector of the State, you have to 
be a person ordinarily resident in that State. Now, several features over the 
functioning of this election system hav e come to notice. In a large number of 
cases, political parties which send repr esentatives from various States, have 
sent a person, who traditionally was not resident in that State, but for the 
purposes of election to the Rajya Sabha, got enrolled as elector in that 
particular State. If we do recollect, about six - seven years ago, there was a 
large controversy whether this practice now requires to be changed, as far as 
the legal system is concerned. We tried to develop a consensus amongst 
political -parties. Some of the political  parties took a particular view that a 
change, perhaps, is now required. Some people still had reservations about 
this. One of the points of criticism which was made against this proposal was 
that this may perhaps affect the spirit of federalism, which is otherwise inherent 
in the fact that it is only an elector of a State who gets elected from that 
particular State. Under the existing syst em or the proposed system, it is the 
Members of the Legislative Assembly of the State who are the electors. It is 
their option whom they choose to elect; who they feel can best represent the 
interests of the State. As against th is, several arguments have been given, 
which I present before the hon. House, as to why this system requires now to 
be altered. One of the first reasons why it requires to be altered is, because in 
the matter of its actual implementation, a breach too frequently was witnessed. 
Therefore, political parties wanted to come to an honest 
244 

[8 April, 2003]                               RAJYA SABHA 
assessment of the situation and come to a conclusion that this, perhaps, now 
requires to be altered itself. The second, under our constitutional scheme, 
under article 19 (1)(e), a person has a right to reside anywhere in the country. 
So, a person who wants to change his residence -- there may be cases where 
people maintain more than one residence, for reasons of business -- for other 
reasons of family, people may be residing in more than one place 
simultaneously. Therefore, this, perhaps may not be in a position to deal with 
such situations, the existing situation. The third reason which was also besides 
the factor of multiple residence is t hat there may be some States where even 
the ruling party or a ruling combination may be unrepresented completely, as 
far as the Lok Sabha is concerned; ma ybe unable to bring Members to the 
Upper House who are among the usual resi dents of that Stat e. Therefore, in 
order to make sure that in the Govern ment also there is representation of 
those States, there may be a compelli ng necessity to get some ordinary 
resident of that State elected from so me other State. It has happened in the 
past; it has happened even today. T here is one particular State which was 
completely unrepresented, otherwise, as far as NDA. is concerned, both in the 
Lok Sabha and the Rajya Sabha. Therefor e, Members got elected from other 
parts of the country, in order to make  sure that those States also got a 
representation in the Council  of Ministers. With thes e facts, the Government 
had introduced this Bill. There were two views even before the Standing 
Committee. 
The second component of this Bill is with regard to the methodology 
of casting their votes amongst the Legislative Assemblies, as far as election to 
the Council of States is concerned. Currently, we have a system where parties 
put up candidates. But we have several ca ses- I have a list of cases, in the 
last few years-where we have certainly seen some kind of unusual practices, 
not very happy for a democracy, which have crept into the polling system. 
Cross-votings have taken place for reasons which are not entirely political. It 
happened in Maharashtra, it happened in  some other States also where 
candidates put up by political parties ha ve lost. In fact, on an earlier occasion, 
I do recollect, when we were discussing the Bill for proxy voting for the armed 
forces, some of the hon. Members of th is House, Mr. Laloo Yadav and others, 
did mention that there is  a great necessity that this procedure itself be 
changed immediately. And,  therefore, after consulting a large number of 
political parties, it has been agreed on this.

RAJYA SABHA                          [8 April, 2003] 
The second proposal is to bring about a change in the methodology 
of voting and the voting, as far as t he Rajya Sabha elections are concerned, 
be now by an open ballot. The procedure for this open ballot, I may state at the 
outset, is not prescribed in the primary le gislation, but would be prescribed as 
far as rules are concerned. The Government, in accordance with those 
procedures, w,ould welcome suggestions  from all Members of the House 
today, in the course of the debate; we  would also, after the Bill is passed, 
welcome suggestions from political parties  subsequently as to what that exact 
procedure could be. We would also consult the Election Commission. 
One procedure which has been sugges ted is, at least the recognised 
political parties, all having polling agents, and those who have been elected as 
Members of the Legislative Assembly on the symbol of that political party, 
would be compelled to show their ballot to the polling agent itself. The rest 
would be then a matter of parties' own discipline. Some Members have even 
made the suggestion whether the Tent h Schedule itself could be extended. 
The Tenth Schedule is a matter which deals with the Legislative Business and 
casting their vote outside, strictly there may not be a need to apply it at this 
stage. Therefore, the consensus built up was, it is not necessary to apply it at 
this stage. 
For the present, the methodology of voting may be converted from a 
secret ballot into an open ballot. The procedure, I can assure this House, we 
will discuss with the political parties, take their suggestions, take the view of 
the Election Commission and only then formulate the procedure. I have given 
one illustration; this is not a firm view  of the Government, but this is one 
possibility. If there are other suggestions, we will welcome those suggestions. 
One point of criticism which has been made against this procedure 
itself has been "secrecy of ballot itse lf is an essential component of every 
election." This is the point some people have made. "And, therefore, 
conversion of a secret ballot into an open ballot may, perhaps, defeat the 
purpose of secrecy." Madam, I wish to co rrect this impression. Elections must 
be fair. In fact, in relation to the Rajya Sabha elections itself, the Supreme 
Court, in 1980, had an occasion to deal with a situation where a vote was 
shown to somebody else and the question raised was that the secrecy had 
been destroyed and, therefore, the election itself got nullified. I 
246 

[8 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
would just read out a paragraph of what  the Supreme Court had said. This is 
the case- I don't think the Member is  present here -of Raghubeer Singh Gill 
versus Sardar Gurucharan Singh Tohra: "The secrecy of ballot was mooted to 
ensure free and fair elections. If the ve ry secrecy of ballot, instead of ensuring 
free and fair elections strikes at the ro ot of the principle of free and fair 
elections, this basic postulate of dem ocracy would be utilised for undoing free 
and fair elections, which is the life an d blood of Parliamentary democracy. If 
secrecy of ballot, instead of ensuring free and fair elections is used, as is done 
in this case, to defeat the very purpose of elections for the purpose for which it 
is enacted, to suppress the wrong coming to light to protect a fraud on the 
election process or even to defend a crime,  that is forgery of ballot paper, this 
principle of secrecy will have to yield to a larger principle of free and fair 
elections." 
Therefore, if secrecy is leading to  a situation where corrupt practices 
have overwhelmingly crept into the sy stem, the question for this House, 
therefore, in this matter would be: Will this principle of secrecy then have to 
yield to openness, which may, perhaps, provide some sunlight, expose those 
who indulge in these practices and then leave it to parties to decide what 
action they want to take against t hem? Openness, therefore, by a large 
number of Members has been felt. The matter went to the Standing 
Committee. It was chaired by hon. Shri Pranab Mukherjee. There were two 
views in the Standing Committee. The Co mmittee, therefore, could not come 
to a firm recommendation as far as this Bill is concerned. After considering the 
recommendations and the various views expressed by the Standing 
Committee, the Government was of the firm  view that it is now time, both to 
change the residence requirement which was a prerequisite condition, as also 
the methodology of voting as far as Rajya Sabha election is concerned in 
order to ensure that the election syst em becomes much cleaner. With these 
words, Madam, I commend to this House that this Bill be considered and 
passed.

As far as the second limb of the amendment is concerned, I wish to 
say this. It is not merely by agreement of political parties. It is extremely 
fashionable today even in the world outside this House to somewhat consider 
that political parties or political indi viduals do everything for their personal 
interest, or some interest of their par ties, or with motives. After all, we 
represent a predominant section of the so ciety. Therefore, when main political 
parties discuss issues, they give their stand to which they may agree or they 
may disagree, they do it in what they fe el the national interest is. Therefore, in 
these cases, the interest is when yo u say that there is an agreement of 
political parties, there is no such agr eement. There are many parties who are 
very close friends of ours, who expr ess reservations here or there about 
certain provisions, it is not that th ey have a motive; they have a genuine 
concern when they have expressed reservations. There is a legitimate concern 
amongst political parties. It is not a ques tion of indiscipline in a political party. 
A question of indiscipline within a political party may arise when there are two 
views in a party and some people decid e that some other candidates should 
be put up. It is a case where we are finding that a trend has started where 
when large amounts are being offered to legislators in the States and amounts 
are so observably large, secrecy is goi ng to conceal that corruption. Merely 
because your vote would not be known, you can quietly take large amounts of 
money as some of the Members pointed out, take it in some cases -- I think, 
Shri Bhandari pointed it out -- from more than one person and then quietly go 
and vote against the political party. Theref ore, what is sought to be checked is

There is one last point, which Shri Bhandariji mentioned. In fact, not 
only Shri Lalu Prasad has mentioned this outside and earlier also, even Shri 
Mulayam Singh Yadav has written a letter that  it is time to consider if what is 
being done in the context of the Rajy a Sabha election should also be 
extended to the Legislat ive Councils. We are examining this matter. We will 
keep this issue open. One of the diffi culties in relation to the Legislative 
Council is that representation to the Legislative Council comes from various 
segments. You have the Graduates c onstituencies, you have some other 
segments, local bodies which are re presented; you also have the State 
Assemblies which elect people. Therefore, to make a regulation only with one 
category of electors and not  the other category of electors, may create some 
complications. But if, in future, a situation does arise that this menace that we 
are seeing in the Rajya Sabha gets extended to the legislative councils, and 
perhaps to one of the cons tituents, that is, the Stat e Assemblies, this House 
would always have the jurisdiction to co nsider the proposal at an appropriate 
stage. With these words, Madam, I recomme nd to this House that this Bill be 
accepted.
